materials.text:
Reading a p-value: the sleep and memory study

A researcher wants to know whether a short nap helps people remember word lists. Forty students are randomly split into two groups. One group naps for 20 minutes after studying a list of 30 words; the other group sits quietly. The nap group recalls 17.1 words on average and the quiet group recalls 14.9. An independent-samples t-test gives p = .03.

What does p = .03 mean? Start with the null hypothesis: in the population, napping makes no difference to recall. The p-value answers one narrow question. If the null hypothesis were true, how often would random sampling alone produce a difference between groups at least as large as the one we observed? Here the answer is about 3 times in 100. The p-value is therefore a statement about the data, assuming the null hypothesis. It is not a statement about the hypothesis.

This is why p = .03 does not mean there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not mean there is a 97% chance that napping works. To say how probable a hypothesis is, we would need extra information that the test does not use, such as how plausible the effect was before the study.

By convention, a p-value below .05 is called statistically significant, and we reject the null hypothesis. That label says nothing about how big or how important the effect is. With thousands of participants, a trivially small difference can produce a tiny p-value. To judge size, look at the effect size (here the difference is 2.2 words, Cohen's d of about 0.7) and at the 95% confidence interval for the difference (0.2 to 4.2 words), which shows how uncertain the estimate is.

Finally, a p-value above .05 does not prove there is no effect. A small study may simply lack the power to detect a real difference. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Report what you found, how big it was, and how sure you can be.

stakes.text: Jordan writes in the lab report that 'there is only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, so napping definitely improves memory a lot'. The marker takes marks off for misinterpreting the test, and Jordan goes on repeating the mistake in their final-year project

preparation.briefing:
Purpose: Practise explaining, in plain words, what a p-value from a two-group study does and does not tell you.
Your role: Your classmate Jordan missed the lecture on the sleep-and-memory study (nap group 17.1 words, quiet group 14.9 words, p = .03) and has a lab report due tomorrow. Help Jordan understand what the result really means, correct anything Jordan gets wrong, and say what else they should look at before deciding whether the nap effect matters.
You will talk to Jordan, who is confident and will push back until your explanation actually makes sense.
Keep in mind: no formulas or calculations are needed. Use the nap study as your example and the material below to check yourself.

turns.text: Before you start: in one sentence, what do you think p = .03 tells you about the nap study?
I think it means that if napping actually did nothing, a difference this big would only happen about 3% of the time by chance, so the result is significant.
Apart from the p-value, what else would you want to know before saying napping 'works'?
How big the difference actually is, like the effect size, and maybe the confidence interval. Also it was only 40 students so I would want to see if it replicates.

Hi, I'm Jordan. I missed the stats lecture and I have to write up the nap study by tomorrow. The output says p = .03. I was going to write 'there's only a 3% chance the result is a fluke', but someone said that's not quite right.
So what does p = .03 actually mean? What is the 3% a percentage of?

It's not the chance the result is a fluke. It's like, if napping really made no difference at all, you'd only get a gap this big between the groups about 3 times out of 100 just from random sampling. So the 3% is assuming the null is true.
Okay, I think I follow. But suppose someone disagreed with you. What would you say to convince them?

Um, I guess I'd say the test starts by assuming there's no effect, so it can't then tell you how likely that assumption is. It only tells you how surprising our data would be if the assumption was true.
Wait, I read somewhere that there's only a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, so a 97% chance that napping really works. Is that right?

Because to know how likely napping does nothing you'd need extra info the test doesn't use, like how believable the effect was before the study even happened. The reading said that. The test just takes the null as given and asks about the data.
Fine, but .03 is a really small number, so the nap effect must be huge, right? Can I write that napping has a big effect on memory?
You already asked me that one. I'd say the same thing really, p is about the data assuming the null, not about the null itself. Did you want to talk about whether the effect is actually big?
Sorry, you're right, you did. Let's move on.
And if it had come out as p = .20, I'd just write that napping does nothing, yeah?

No, a small p doesn't mean a big effect. With a huge sample even a tiny difference can get a tiny p. You'd have to look at the effect size, here it's 2.2 words and Cohen's d about 0.7, which I think is medium to large-ish but I'm not totally sure on the cutoffs.
Oh, that's useful, it answers something I was going to ask. And if it had come out as p = .20, I'd just write that napping does nothing, yeah?

I'd point them to the confidence interval too. It goes from 0.2 to 4.2 words, so the real effect could be pretty tiny or quite big, we're not that sure. So I wouldn't write 'big effect', more like there's a difference but the size is uncertain.
Oh, that's useful, it answers something I was going to ask. And if it had come out as p = .20, I'd just write that napping does nothing, yeah?

No, a non-significant p doesn't prove there's no effect. With only 40 people the study might not have enough power to pick up a real difference. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, so you'd just say you didn't find a significant difference.
What would happen if that weren't the case?
Honestly I think I've covered it. For your report just say what you found, how big it was and how sure you can be. Good luck with it!
Thank you. I think I could explain some of this to someone else now.

I think it went okay. I was happiest with explaining the 3% is about the data if the null is true, not the chance it is a fluke. Jordan kept asking the same question though so it got a bit repetitive.
What would you do differently if you did it again?
I would explain the confidence interval more clearly and maybe check the Cohen d cutoffs before saying medium or large. I was a bit vague there.

With 6,000 pupils even a really tiny improvement could come out significant, so p = .04 does not tell you if it is worth paying for. I would want to know how many marks it actually improves scores by and the confidence interval. I would also check who ran the study, I guess, since that is not really from this session.
